titleOptions: IKEA Was Banned From Furniture Fairs. So It Built This.
How a Table Leg Created a $50 Billion Empire
hook: In the 1950s, Sweden's furniture industry tried to kill a young upstart. Suppliers were pressured to stop selling to him, and he was shut out of trade fairs. That boycott is the reason almost every home on Earth now has a piece of IKEA in it.

beats.heading: Cold open: the boycott
beats.narration: Sweden's furniture industry tries to shut out one stubborn young seller.

beats.heading: A boy who sold matches
beats.narration: Ingvar Kamprad starts trading at five and founds IKEA at seventeen.

beats.heading: The price war
beats.narration: Cheap mail-order furniture triggers a price war and a quality crisis, and the first showroom fixes it.

beats.heading: The table leg
beats.narration: One employee removes the legs from a table to fit it in a car, and flat-pack is born.

beats.heading: Turning the boycott into a weapon
beats.narration: Banned by suppliers, IKEA designs its own furniture and finds its own factories.

beats.heading: The machine
beats.narration: Self-service warehouses, the maze, the meatballs: a system designed around one idea, low prices.

beats.heading: The lesson
beats.narration: Constraints didn't slow IKEA down. They became the business model.

scenes.narration: In the 1950s, Sweden's furniture industry tried to kill a young upstart.
scenes.visual: Archive black-and-white photos of 1950s Swedish furniture showrooms; ominous low strings.

scenes.narration: Suppliers were pressured to stop selling to him, and he was shut out of trade fairs.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: a map of Sweden with factories lighting up red and lines to one small dot being cut.

scenes.narration: That boycott is the reason almost every home on Earth now has a piece of IKEA in it.
scenes.visual: Fast montage of stock footage: flat-pack boxes, an Allen key, a family assembling a bookshelf.

scenes.narration: This is the story of how a teenager from a Swedish farm turned every disadvantage into the world's biggest furniture company.
scenes.visual: Title card: BUILT & BROKEN, IKEA, over a rural Swedish farm landscape.

scenes.narration: Ingvar Kamprad grew up on a farm called Elmtaryd, near the village of Agunnaryd, in Småland, a poor, rocky region of southern Sweden known for thrifty people.
scenes.visual: Map zoom into Småland, Sweden; stock footage of red wooden farmhouses and stone walls.

scenes.narration: He started selling early. As a boy, he bought matches in bulk in Stockholm and sold them one box at a time to neighbours at a profit.
scenes.visual: Illustrated 1930s boy on a bicycle with a box of matches on a country road.

scenes.narration: Then fish, Christmas cards, seeds and pencils. Anything he could buy cheap and sell for a little more.
scenes.visual: Kinetic text listing products, each popping in with a small price tag.

scenes.narration: In 1943, at seventeen, he registered his own company. He named it using his initials and the farm and village he grew up in: Ingvar Kamprad, Elmtaryd, Agunnaryd. I K E A.
scenes.visual: Animated letters I, K, E, A assembling from the words Ingvar, Kamprad, Elmtaryd, Agunnaryd.

scenes.narration: At first IKEA had nothing to do with furniture. It sold pens, wallets, picture frames and watches by mail order, delivered by the local milk van.
scenes.visual: Archive-style photo of a 1940s milk truck on a gravel road; product illustrations floating out of it.

scenes.narration: In 1948 Kamprad noticed that local factories made good furniture cheaply, and he added it to his catalogue. It sold so well that he soon dropped almost everything else.
scenes.visual: Animated catalogue page flipping, small items fading out as chairs and tables take over.

scenes.narration: In 1951 he published the first IKEA catalogue. But mail-order furniture had a problem.
scenes.visual: Generic illustrated 1950s mail-order catalogue cover on a kitchen table (no real IKEA artwork).

scenes.narration: IKEA and a rival were locked in a price war, cutting prices again and again. And when prices fall, quality usually falls with them.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: two price tags racing downward, a chair beside them getting visibly flimsier.

scenes.narration: Customers couldn't touch the furniture before ordering. Complaints piled up. Kamprad's whole business was in danger.
scenes.visual: Stack of complaint letters animating onto a desk; a wobbly chair leg snapping.

scenes.narration: His fix was simple and brilliant. In 1953 he opened a showroom in the town of Älmhult, so people could see, sit on and compare the furniture before they bought it.
scenes.visual: Illustrated 1950s showroom interior with families testing sofas, warm daylight.

scenes.narration: Now IKEA could compete on value instead of just price. Customers could see why the cheaper chair was the better deal.
scenes.visual: Split screen: two chairs with price tags; the IKEA one gets a gold check mark.

scenes.narration: And that is exactly when the established furniture industry decided IKEA had to be stopped.
scenes.visual: Slow push-in on a dark boardroom table with cigar smoke, 1950s style, illustrated.

scenes.narration: Competitors pressured manufacturers to stop supplying IKEA, and IKEA was barred from selling at a major furniture fair. Without suppliers, a furniture shop has nothing to sell.
scenes.visual: Map graphic: supplier lines to IKEA turning red and snapping one by one.

scenes.narration: Most small companies would have died here. IKEA did two things instead, and both of them still define the company today.
scenes.visual: Kinetic text: TWO DECISIONS, with the numbers 1 and 2 dropping in.

scenes.narration: Decision one: if nobody will sell us furniture, we'll design our own. IKEA began creating products in-house, so it controlled the design, the cost and the materials.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of a designer sketching furniture on paper, then a 3D wireframe chair rotating.

scenes.narration: Decision two: if Swedish factories won't make it, we'll find factories that will. In the early 1960s, IKEA turned to manufacturers in Poland, where costs were far lower.
scenes.visual: Animated map line from Sweden across the Baltic Sea to Poland, factories lighting up gold.

scenes.narration: The boycott that was meant to starve IKEA ended up handing it the two things that would make it unbeatable: its own designs and a cheaper supply chain.
scenes.visual: Gold crack effect turning into a gold arrow pointing up.

scenes.narration: Around the same time came the most famous accident in furniture history.
scenes.visual: Slow-motion stock shot of a car boot opening in daylight.

scenes.narration: In 1956, an IKEA designer named Gillis Lundgren was trying to fit a table into a car after a photo shoot. It wouldn't go in. So he took the legs off.
scenes.visual: Illustration: a 1950s man unscrewing table legs beside a small car, table top leaning against it.

scenes.narration: That small moment sparked the idea that changed everything: what if furniture shipped flat, and the customer put it together at home?
scenes.visual: Animated exploded view of a table separating into flat parts and stacking into a box.

scenes.narration: Flat packs take a fraction of the space. More fit in every truck and every warehouse, and fewer break in transport. Every one of those savings goes into a lower price.
scenes.visual: Motion graphic: a truck filled with assembled furniture vs the same truck stacked with flat packs, counter showing how many more fit.

scenes.narration: And it turned the customer into part of the workforce. You pick it up. You carry it home. You build it. IKEA saves on labour, and you save on price.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of a couple carrying boxes to a car, then laughing while assembling a shelf.

scenes.narration: In 1965, IKEA opened a giant store outside Stockholm. So many people came that staff couldn't keep up, so the manager opened the warehouse and let customers fetch products themselves.
scenes.visual: Archive-style photo of crowds outside a large 1960s store; animated arrows pointing into a warehouse.

scenes.narration: Self-service became the IKEA model. The showroom shows you the dream, the warehouse hands you the box.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of a big-box warehouse aisle with tall shelving, shoppers with flat trolleys.

scenes.narration: Every detail of the modern store serves the same goal. The one-way path walks you past every department. The restaurant keeps you shopping longer. The cheap hot dog at the exit leaves you with a good last memory.
scenes.visual: Animated top-down floor plan with a winding one-way arrow path; icons for restaurant and exit food stand.

scenes.narration: Even the product names are a system. Swedish words and place names, sorted by category, so a name tells staff what kind of product it is.
scenes.visual: Kinetic text of invented Swedish-sounding product names sliding into labelled category boxes.

scenes.narration: Kamprad himself became famous for thrift. He flew economy, drove an old Volvo for years, and told staff that wasting resources was a mortal sin at IKEA.
scenes.visual: Stock footage of an old Volvo estate on a country road; economy airplane cabin.

scenes.narration: IKEA expanded across Europe through the 1970s, then North America, Asia and the Middle East.
scenes.visual: Animated world map with store pins appearing decade by decade, counter rising.

scenes.narration: Today the IKEA brand has more than four hundred and fifty stores in over sixty markets, and yearly sales measured in the tens of billions of euros.
scenes.visual: Big kinetic numbers: 450+ STORES, 60+ MARKETS over a timelapse of a store car park.

scenes.narration: The company Kamprad built is also unusually structured. Most of IKEA is owned by foundations, designed so the business could never be easily sold off or broken up.
scenes.visual: Simple motion graphic of a company box sitting inside a foundation box, with a lock icon.

scenes.narration: IKEA's history has its controversies too, from Kamprad's admitted youthful political ties, which he later called the greatest mistake of his life, to questions about suppliers and forests. Size brings scrutiny.
scenes.visual: Muted archive newspaper texture with blurred headlines; no identifiable people.

scenes.narration: Ingvar Kamprad died in 2018 at the age of ninety-one.
scenes.visual: Quiet shot of a Småland forest at dawn, text: 1926 to 2018.

scenes.narration: Look back at the turning points. A price war forced the showroom. A boycott forced in-house design and cheaper factories. A table that wouldn't fit in a car created flat-pack.
scenes.visual: Animated timeline with each turning point lighting gold: 1953, the boycott, 1956.

scenes.narration: None of those ideas came from a strategy meeting. Each one came from a problem that should have hurt IKEA.
scenes.visual: Kinetic text: EVERY PROBLEM BECAME A FEATURE.

scenes.narration: That's the real lesson. The people trying to stop IKEA didn't slow it down. They designed its business model for it.
scenes.visual: Final shot: a flat-pack box on a doorstep at sunset, slowly pushing in.

outro: Next on Built & Broken: Netflix lost 800,000 subscribers in a single quarter by attacking its own business, and it was the smartest thing it ever did. Subscribe so you don't miss it.
